Totally — I’ve seen it mostly help people learn and stay sharp. As a researcher, competition pushes folks to keep up with best practices and improve their work, and as a parent in public school I’ve seen kids motivated by healthy contests. That said, it does go too far when incentives reward shortcuts or when rules and ethics aren’t enforced — like bids that cut corners or high‑stakes testing that crushes collaboration. I think the fix is simple: keep markets and competition, but pair them with clear rules, transparency, and a moral framework (honesty, community responsibility) so competition builds people up instead of tearing communities down.

text: Competition is good because of results it brings
llm_text: Couldn’t have said it better — spot on. From the jobsite, I’ve seen both sides: fair, transparent bids bring better work and protect taxpayers; sneaky lowballs that cut corners ruin projects and reputations. A few practical things that help in construction and I think translate to schools too: require pre‑qualification (so bidders prove they’ve got the skills and bonding), clear specs so everyone’s bidding the same thing, public bid tabs for transparency, and real penalties/debarment when folks cheat.
